messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Car Similarity: Similar cars, Crowding: Crowded places
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Face Hiding: cover face with hands

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Weber was 33 when he came to treatment, a divorced white American man who worked as a graphic designer for a small branding firm. He described the event he could not stop organizing his life around as an encounter with police late at night after leaving a friend’s apartment. He had been driving home in the dark through a downtown area after midnight, tired and eager to get back to his apartment, when flashing lights appeared behind him. He remembered the patrol car pulling up at an angle, the hard spill of headlights and red-blue light into his car, and the way everything outside the windows suddenly looked both glaring and unreal. What stayed with him most was not a full, orderly narrative, but a set of moments that still felt immediate: the shape of the police car beside him, the officer approaching with a weapon visible at his side, the shouted commands, the sense that there were too many bodies too close to him in too little space. He had covered his face with his hands at one point, partly from panic, partly because he felt exposed and trapped, and he still remembered thinking that if he moved wrong in that darkness, something terrible would happen.

In the weeks afterward, Daniel found that night had changed meaning for him. He dreaded the period between evening and sleep, and if he woke in the dark he would lie still for a moment with a jolt of alarm before orienting himself. What frightened him most was how quickly the feeling came back, as if darkness itself meant danger. Driving became narrower and more calculated. If he noticed a car that looked like the one from that night—a similar model, similar light bar, even a similar silhouette in his rearview mirror—his body tightened immediately. He would grip the wheel, check mirrors repeatedly, or change routes just to get away from it. In crowded places, especially when people moved around him unpredictably, he felt the same trapped pressure he had felt by the roadside with officers close to his door. He began stepping out of grocery lines, skipping packed bars and concerts, and timing errands for quieter hours.

Daniel’s work life gave these reactions a daily stage. The design firm expected in-person collaboration, and their office sat in a busy commercial district where lunch meant crowded sidewalks and cafés. He started eating at his desk to avoid the rush downstairs. When the team wanted to meet a new client at a bustling restaurant, he often found an excuse to stay back and “finish revisions.” On more than one occasion he had to walk past uniformed police officers stationed near a downtown event, and he would immediately turn his face away or bring his hands up, partly covering it as he passed. He knew it looked odd, but the sight of uniforms, holsters, and weapons felt intolerable. He had come to believe that being seen by police was dangerous in itself, that attention from them could turn without warning into another night like that one.

Over the following months, Daniel increasingly relied on alcohol and whatever medication or drugs were available to him to get through evenings and to blunt the edge of waking in the dark. He told himself he needed something to shut his mind off before bed and something to take the edge off after difficult days downtown. Sometimes after spotting a similar car on his commute, he would go straight home and drink rather than risk being out again. The pattern narrowed his life. He became less dependable with friends because he declined invitations if they involved crowds, and after his divorce he was living alone with few people who saw how much of his day was arranged around not being triggered. At work he was still talented, but coworkers had begun to notice that he avoided client events, preferred remote contact whenever possible, and seemed visibly tense if there was police presence outside the building.

By the time he sought help, Daniel was exhausted by how small his world had become. What finally pushed him into treatment was a recent night when he woke in a dark apartment, disoriented and panicked, and then called in sick the next morning after seeing a police car that resembled the one from the stop near his office. He said he was tired of planning every route, every errand, and every social interaction around what he might see. At the same time, he was certain that letting his guard down would be reckless. He wanted help because he did not want to keep drinking his way through nights and hiding from uniforms and crowds, but he was afraid that talking about what happened would make him feel as trapped and exposed as he had on the roadside. What he hoped for, in the plainest terms, was to be able to wake up in the dark and know he was only in his own room, to drive without scanning every similar car, and to move through his city without feeling that danger was waiting just behind him.
